sections.guidingQuestion: How can cells from the same fertilized egg become different?
sections.explanation:
Fertilization produces a zygote, which divides repeatedly to generate initially unspecialized descendant cells. As the embryo develops, cells occupy different positions relative to surrounding tissues and molecular signals. Some signalling molecules (morphogens) form concentration gradients, so cells in different positions experience different concentrations even while inheriting essentially the same genome.

Cells interpret those graded signals through regulatory pathways that increase or decrease expression of particular genes. Changes in protein abundance and activity then direct differentiation into particular cell types. A high or low morphogen concentration is not itself a different gene; it is contextual information that helps select a cell fate. Because the same genome can support distinct expression programs, a tissue may contain cells with different morphology and roles. Embryogenesis is regulated, not random conversion into arbitrary cell types.

Try drawing three embryonic cells at positions along a signalling gradient, then sketch one graph of morphogen concentration against position. Thresholds and regulatory networks can cause different sets of genes to be expressed in cells above and below a particular signal concentration. These responses also depend on cell competence and previous developmental history, not signal concentration alone. A predicted outcome should connect position, regulatory change and morphological differentiation, rather than saying a chemical directly turns into a tissue.

Two embryonic cells inherit essentially the same DNA but experience different morphogen concentrations. Signal-dependent transcription factors can switch different gene sets on or off; the resulting differentiation is not normally explained by wholesale changes to their DNA sequences.
sections.revisionSummary: Morphogen concentration gradients can alter expression patterns and influence early cell fates. Position-dependent signals alter gene expression while the inherited genome usually remains the same.

embryo: an organism in early development
morphogen: signal whose concentration can influence cell fate
gene expression: use of genetic information to make a functional RNA or protein
differentiation: development of specialized cellular features and functions

sections.guidingQuestion: What makes a stem cell different from a mature specialized cell?
sections.explanation:
Two capacities define stem cells: self-renewal and differentiation. Self-renewal means cell divisions can yield daughters that retain stem-cell properties; differentiation yields descendants that acquire specialized characteristics. In appropriate biological contexts or culture conditions, stem-cell lineages can undergo extensive or ongoing division. Their capacities are regulated by genetic programs, cellular surroundings and signals, rather than guaranteeing that every stem cell literally proliferates forever.

Some stem cells divide to replace cells lost from continuously renewed tissues, while others may be relatively quiescent until they receive activating signals. A mature red blood cell cannot divide and is not a stem cell; a bone marrow hematopoietic stem cell can produce both renewing daughters and blood progenitors. Do not confuse potency (range of possible differentiated descendants) with the current speed of division or the number of years a cell survives.

Think about lineage outcomes instead of assuming every division has two identical fates. One division may leave a daughter in the stem-cell pool and produce a progenitor that progressively specializes; in other contexts, divisions can expand or deplete the pool. Stem-cell capacity is tested through lineage evidence under appropriate conditions. 'Unlimited division' in introductory models refers to enduring self-renewal potential in favorable conditions, not immortality of every individual stem cell or absence of senescence and regulation.

A stem-cell division can leave at least one daughter with stem-cell potential while another progresses toward a specialized lineage. Self-renewal maintains the population; differentiation produces functionally different descendants. Not every daughter must remain unspecialized forever.

self-renewal: production of descendants that retain stem-cell properties
differentiation: development of specialized cellular features and functions
potency: range of cell types a cell can generate under suitable conditions

sections.guidingQuestion: How does location control adult stem cell activity?
sections.explanation:
An adult stem-cell niche is a localized microenvironment that helps preserve a stem-cell population or stimulates proliferation and differentiation when tissue replacement is needed. Signals come from neighboring cells, extracellular materials and local chemical conditions. The niche is more than the stem cell itself: it provides regulatory cues that influence whether daughter cells remain stem-like, multiply, or differentiate.

In bone marrow, hematopoietic stem cells are supported by surrounding stromal and vascular components that regulate blood cell renewal. In hair follicles, stem cells occupy regions associated with hair renewal and can respond to local niche signals during cycles of growth. Both examples show that stem cell behavior is context-dependent. Leaving or damaging a niche can alter cell behavior; this does not mean that every external tissue instantly becomes a stem-cell niche.

Compare how the marrow and follicle microenvironments maintain their resident stem cells. A niche may supply contact-dependent signals, extracellular matrix attachment and soluble factors; removing a cell from that context can change its behavior. Blood-cell production must be sustained throughout adult life, while hair growth follows cycles involving periods of activity and relative quiescence. The scientific distinction is between cells' potential to differentiate and the niche's influence on whether they remain inactive, self-renew or commit to a new lineage.

Bone-marrow and hair-follicle niches provide localized interactions and signals. Depending on physiological need, a niche can preserve a relatively quiescent stem-cell pool or promote proliferation and differentiation; a niche is not merely an empty physical hole.
sections.revisionSummary: Bone marrow and hair follicles provide adult human examples of regulated niches. It is a functional tissue microenvironment that regulates stem-cell maintenance, proliferation and differentiation.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why do totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent mean different things?
sections.explanation:
Very early embryonic cells can be totipotent, producing embryonic and supporting extraembryonic tissues. Pluripotent cells can give rise to many different body cell types but not the whole set of extraembryonic tissues. Multipotent adult stem cells, such as those in bone marrow, are restricted to a smaller range of related lineages. These categories measure potential differentiation outcomes, not how large a cell is or how many times it can divide.

Multipotent adult tissue stem cells generate a more limited family of descendants. A hematopoietic stem cell in bone marrow can ultimately produce several types of blood cell, but ordinarily not neural tissue. In an early animal embryo, developmental potential becomes restricted as embryonic lineages separate. The inner cell mass of a mammalian blastocyst contains pluripotent progenitors, not a cluster of uniformly totipotent cells. Potency and differentiation state are related but distinct measurements.

Apply potency classifications to a lineage tree. Start from a zygote with the broadest natural developmental potential, then consider pluripotent cells within an early embryo and progressively restricted adult blood stem cells. Ask whether the descendants could contribute to the extraembryonic supporting tissues as well as embryonic tissue: that distinguishes totipotency from pluripotency. The experimental method and developmental stage matter; do not describe all cells of a later blastocyst as totipotent simply because the zygote once was.

A totipotent early embryonic cell can generate embryo and supporting extraembryonic lineages; pluripotent cells can generate many body cell types but generally not an entire viable organism alone; multipotent adult stem cells produce a more restricted lineage range.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why are human specialized cells so different in size?
sections.explanation:
Human cells vary greatly in their dimensions and shape because they perform different functions. A mature human erythrocyte is a small flexible biconcave disc that can pass through narrow capillaries, whereas a mature human egg cell has a large volume and cytoplasmic resources important for early development. Sperm are smaller cells with a compact head and flagellum for movement through the female reproductive tract. White blood cells vary in size, shape and behavior according to type.

A neuron can have a very long axon, enabling communication over large anatomical distances, while a skeletal muscle fibre may extend over centimeters as a long multinucleate contractile cell. Their linear length should not be mistaken for a comparably huge spherical volume. Size changes diffusion distances and supply demands, but cell function also depends on membrane folding, internal transport, metabolic activity and tissue context. There is no single 'best' size across every cell type.

Separate length from volume when comparing human cells. A neuron can extend a thin axon over substantial distance, but that does not mean its entire cytoplasm fills an equally wide cylinder. A skeletal muscle fibre is long and usually contains many peripheral nuclei. Human sperm, erythrocytes and oocytes also differ in shape, cytoplasmic contents and life-cycle stage. Record whether a measurement refers to diameter, length or volume, and avoid using a single average measurement to represent every cell in a mixed tissue.

Human erythrocytes are small and deformable, sperm have a compact motile form, the ovum is much larger, neurons can extend long processes and skeletal muscle fibres are long multinucleate cells. Describe relevant dimensions rather than assuming every cell is spherical.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why does increasing linear size reduce relative exchange area?
sections.explanation:
For a cube with side length L, surface area = 6L² and volume = L³, so the ratio SA:V = 6/L. A cube of side 1 µm has 6 µm² surface area and 1 µm³ volume, giving 6:1 µm⁻¹. At side 2 µm, area is 24 µm² and volume 8 µm³, ratio 3:1 µm⁻¹. At side 4 µm, area is 96 µm² and volume 64 µm³, ratio 1.5:1 µm⁻¹. Doubling size multiplies area by four but volume by eight.

Substances cross the cell membrane across surface area, while total requirements for nutrients, gas exchange and waste clearance often increase with metabolically active volume. Therefore, if membrane exchange capacity per unit area and demand per volume stayed equal, a larger cell would have less exchange capacity relative to demand. Real cells are not cubes: folds, shape, transport proteins, metabolic rates and cytoplasmic organization alter performance. The cube model isolates the scaling rule without claiming that every biological limitation has one simple cause.

Derive the relationship instead of memorizing a table. Scale every linear dimension of a cube by k: each face area scales by k², six faces together also scale by k², but volume scales by k³. Consequently the SA:V numerical ratio is multiplied by 1/k. SA:V has dimensions of inverse length when numerical area and volume use coherent units. In real cells, membrane transport capacity depends on proteins and conditions and metabolism need not rise exactly with volume; explain these qualifications whenever you predict exchange limits.

A cube with side 5 µm has surface area 6 × 25 = 150 µm² and volume 125 µm³, so SA:V = 1.2 µm⁻¹. When side doubles to 10 µm, the ratio halves to 0.6 µm⁻¹, even though total surface area rises.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which structural adaptations increase surface area relative to cell volume? (HL)
sections.explanation:
Flattening a cell increases surface area relative to its volume for a given amount of internal material and can shorten diffusion distance. A mature human red blood cell's biconcave shape makes a relatively high membrane area accessible to gas exchange, while its thin central region reduces diffusion path length. A flattened shape is not the only possible adaptation, and erythrocytes also rely on hemoglobin and flexibility.

Microvilli are membrane projections that increase exchange surface area, as on epithelial cells of the proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron. Invaginations are inward folds of the membrane that create additional membrane area without equivalent increases in total cellular volume. Both adaptations are meaningful when the appropriate exchange/transport proteins are present; more membrane alone does not guarantee unlimited transport. Distinguish microvilli from motile cilia and describe the physical geometry involved.

Compare how shape changes exchange. A biconcave erythrocyte offers a useful surface-to-volume geometry and a short central diffusion path, while the proximal convoluted tubule adds extensive apical microvilli for reabsorption. Infoldings can enlarge membrane area elsewhere in a cell. Ask which membrane face contacts the relevant fluid and what transport proteins it contains: enlarging an inaccessible or transporter-free region might not improve the needed exchange. Microvilli are not propulsive flagella, and the kidney example should not be confused with intestinal absorption.

A red blood cell's biconcavity improves relative exchange area and deformability; proximal nephron epithelial microvilli expand the apical exchange surface, while basolateral infoldings support substantial membrane-associated transport. A microvillus does not create extra cytoplasmic volume proportionally.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why do alveoli need both type I and type II pneumocytes? (HL)
sections.explanation:
Type I pneumocytes are extremely thin and reduce diffusion distance for respiratory gases. Type II pneumocytes contain numerous lamellar bodies, which release surfactant into alveoli. Surfactant reduces surface tension and helps alveoli remain open. The two differentiated cell types combine gas diffusion and surface stability in one epithelial tissue; type II pneumocytes should not be drawn as the thin majority of the diffusion barrier.

Type II pneumocytes release surfactant into the alveolar lumen. Surfactant reduces surface tension at the air–liquid interface and helps keep alveoli from collapsing during breathing. The thin barrier produced by type I cells and surfactant secretion by type II cells are related to the overall function of the tissue, but must not be confused: type I is not the principal surfactant secretor. Lamellar bodies represent intracellular secretory structure; they are not empty alveolar air spaces. Diagram thickness is exaggerated for visibility and not a literal microscopic scale.

Treat the alveolar wall as a cooperative tissue. Type I cells form expansive very thin sheets that reduce the distance gases diffuse; capillary endothelium and a basement membrane contribute additional layers to the blood-air barrier. Type II cells are more cuboidal and package surfactant in lamellar bodies before secretion. Surface tension at the wet alveolar lining opposes expansion; surfactant decreases it. A diagram should deliberately exaggerate thin membranes for visibility, then state that the drawing has no measured tissue thickness.

Type I pneumocytes minimize diffusion distance, while type II cells package pulmonary surfactant in lamellar bodies and secrete it. Loss of surfactant raises surface tension and makes alveoli more prone to collapse without making type I cells thicker.

sections.guidingQuestion: How does muscle cellular organization support different contraction patterns? (HL)
sections.explanation:
Both cardiac muscle cells and skeletal striated muscle fibres contain contractile myofibrils built of repeated sarcomeres. Cardiac muscle cells usually branch, connect end-to-end through intercalated discs and typically have one central nucleus, although some are binucleate. Their network assists coordinated rhythmic contraction. Skeletal muscle fibres are long, generally unbranched structures formed by fusion of myoblasts; they contain many nuclei positioned near their periphery.

A skeletal striated muscle fibre is a single highly specialized multinucleated cell, not a string of numerous ordinary single-nucleus cells. The relative length, branching and nuclei number are part of structural explanations for tissue function, but students should distinguish observations from proposed functional hypotheses. Both tissues appear striated because of the organization of myofibrils. Neither should be depicted as merely an elongated generic animal cell with a single oval nucleus.

Formulate an evidence-based hypothesis: branching and intercalated discs in cardiac cells support transmission of forces and electrical signals through a functional network; long fused skeletal fibres permit coordinated shortening along their axis. Both have organized myofibrils and repeating sarcomeres, so striation alone cannot distinguish them. A cardiac section may show centrally situated nuclei and distinct junctions; a skeletal fibre may have numerous peripheral nuclei. Identify whether a long multinucleated object represents one fused cell or several joined cardiomyocytes before drawing conclusions.

Cardiac muscle cells are typically short, branching and have one or occasionally two central nuclei, helping them form connected contractile networks. Skeletal striated fibres are long, generally unbranched syncytia with many peripheral nuclei; both contain myofibrils.

sections.guidingQuestion: How are sperm and egg cells adapted for fertilization and early development? (HL)
sections.explanation:
A human sperm cell is comparatively small and motile. It has a streamlined head containing a haploid nucleus and an acrosome with proteins involved in interacting with the egg's surrounding layers. Mitochondria concentrated in the midpiece support energy demands of flagellar movement, while the flagellum generates propulsion. These features help sperm reach and interact with the egg and deliver paternal genetic material.

A human secondary oocyte is large and nonmotile, with a haploid chromosome complement arrested at metaphase II until fertilization triggers completion of meiosis. Its abundant cytoplasm supplies molecules and machinery to the early embryo; its plasma membrane and surrounding zona pellucida participate in fertilization interactions. Egg size should not be attributed to containing much more DNA than the sperm: both gametes carry haploid nuclear genomes. Simplified drawings should not show an adult ovulated human egg as already having completed meiosis II before fertilization.

Connect each gamete adaptation to its function without implying one gamete contributes all the important genetic information. A human sperm's acrosome participates in reaching and interacting with the oocyte, its midpiece supplies energy for movement, and its flagellum produces motility. The ovulated secondary oocyte has a large cytoplasm and protective extracellular coat, and contributes cellular machinery needed by the developing embryo. Both contribute haploid nuclear genetic material; extra molecular detail on gamete recognition should be treated as supporting context, not an unrelated assessed requirement.

A human sperm uses acrosomal enzymes and a flagellum during fertilization; its midpiece contains mitochondria. The ovulated human secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II, so show chromosomes on a spindle rather than incorrectly drawing an intact diploid oocyte nucleus.

questions.prompt: Removing a marrow stem cell from its surrounding support cells changes its behaviour. Which explanation best describes the role of its niche?

options.text: Bone marrow contains only mature red blood cells.
options.feedback: Bone marrow contains blood-forming stem and progenitor cells.

options.text: Bone marrow and hair follicles provide adult human examples of regulated niches.
options.feedback: Correct. Bone marrow and hair follicles provide adult human examples of regulated niches.

options.text: The niche has no effect on stem cell fate.
options.feedback: Local cell-cell and extracellular signals influence renewal.

options.text: Every adult body cell sits in a stem-cell niche.
options.feedback: A niche is a specific regulatory environment, not every tissue location.

questions.prompt: An early embryonic cell can contribute to embryonic and extraembryonic tissues, whereas a marrow stem cell produces blood lineages. How do their developmental potentials compare?

options.text: Stem cell potency is identical to its cell division rate.
options.feedback: Potency concerns developmental range, not how frequently a cell divides.

options.text: Totipotent potential is broader than pluripotent, which is broader than multipotent.
options.feedback: Correct. Totipotent potential is broader than pluripotent, which is broader than multipotent.

options.text: Adult blood stem cells are totipotent.
options.feedback: Adult hematopoietic stem cells have lineage-limited multipotency.

options.text: Pluripotent cells can only make red blood cells.
options.feedback: Pluripotent cells can differentiate into derivatives of all germ layers.

questions.prompt: A neuron has a long thin axon, while a secondary oocyte has a large cell body. Which interpretation avoids confusing length with volume?

options.text: Cell shape and dimensions reflect function: erythrocytes, gametes, neurons and skeletal fibres differ.
options.feedback: Correct. Cell shape and dimensions reflect function: erythrocytes, gametes, neurons and skeletal fibres differ.

options.text: A sperm's flagellum is mainly for storing the embryo's cytoplasm.
options.feedback: The sperm tail is primarily a motility structure.

options.text: All white blood cells are exactly the diameter of red blood cells.
options.feedback: White blood cells encompass variable morphologies.

options.text: Neurons must be spherical because axons are long.
options.feedback: Neurons often have elongated processes and irregular bodies.

questions.prompt: A cube model has side length 2 µm and all six faces exposed. What are its surface area, volume and surface-area-to-volume ratio?

options.text: 12 µm²; 8 µm³; 1.5 µm⁻¹
options.feedback: This halves the surface area: a cube has six faces, each of area 2² = 4 µm², giving 24 µm².

options.text: 24 µm²; 4 µm³; 6 µm⁻¹
options.feedback: The volume must use three dimensions: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 µm³. Four is the area of one face, not the volume.

options.text: 8 µm²; 24 µm³; 0.33 µm⁻¹
options.feedback: Area and volume have been interchanged. Surface area is 6 × 2² = 24 µm²; volume is 2³ = 8 µm³.

options.text: 24 µm²; 8 µm³; 3 µm⁻¹
options.feedback: Six faces each have area 4 µm²; volume is 2³ = 8 µm³. Dividing area by volume gives 3 µm⁻¹.

questions.prompt: A proximal tubule cell develops many apical microvilli while its volume changes little. Which explanation predicts improved exchange capacity?

options.text: Microvilli are always powered by the same motility machinery as cilia.
options.feedback: Microvilli contain actin-based structure and are not motile cilia.

options.text: Invagination necessarily removes membrane area.
options.feedback: Membrane folds can expand accessible surface area.

options.text: Flattening, microvilli and invagination can increase effective membrane surface relative to volume.
options.feedback: Correct. Flattening, microvilli and invagination can increase effective membrane surface relative to volume.

options.text: Cell walls double the volume without any extra membrane.
options.feedback: The adaptations concern cell geometry and membrane surface.

questions.prompt: A lung sample has very thin cells beside cuboidal cells containing lamellar bodies. Which functional assignment is supported?

options.text: Both are identical cells with different names.
options.feedback: They have distinct morphology, organelles and function.

options.text: Surfactant increases alveolar surface tension.
options.feedback: Surfactant reduces surface tension and helps prevent alveolar collapse.

options.text: Type I cells are thick glands holding lamellar vesicles.
options.feedback: Type II pneumocytes have the prominent surfactant storage organelles.

options.text: Type I pneumocytes shorten gas diffusion distance, while type II release surfactant to lower surface tension.
options.feedback: Correct. Type I pneumocytes shorten gas diffusion distance, while type II release surfactant to lower surface tension.

questions.prompt: Two striated muscle samples differ: one has short branched cells with central nuclei; the other has long unbranched multinucleated fibres. Which interpretation is supported?

options.text: Every cardiomyocyte contains ten peripheral nuclei.
options.feedback: Cardiac cells usually have one or two central nuclei.

options.text: Only cardiac cells contain myofibrils.
options.feedback: Skeletal striated muscle also has myofibrils.

options.text: Cardiac cells are typically branched with central nuclei; skeletal fibres are long, unbranched and multinucleated.
options.feedback: Correct. Cardiac cells are typically branched with central nuclei; skeletal fibres are long, unbranched and multinucleated.

options.text: Skeletal muscle fibres lack striations.
options.feedback: Skeletal fibres are striated through organized sarcomeres.

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly links the structures of human sperm and an ovulated secondary oocyte to their functions?

options.text: A mature human secondary oocyte has completed meiosis II before fertilization.
options.feedback: The ovulated oocyte generally completes meiosis II following fertilization.

options.text: Sperm have motility-related structures; the oocyte provides substantial cytoplasm for early development.
options.feedback: Correct. Sperm have motility-related structures; the oocyte provides substantial cytoplasm for early development.

options.text: Sperm cells have no genetic material.
options.feedback: A sperm head carries a haploid nucleus.

options.text: The human oocyte swims using a flagellum.
options.feedback: The human oocyte is nonmotile and lacks a sperm-like flagellum.

questions.prompt: A cubic model cell has side length 5 µm. Calculate the surface area, volume and surface-area-to-volume ratio, then predict the ratio after doubling its side length. Explain one consequence for exchange.
questions.answer: A = 6 × 5² = 150 µm²; V = 5³ = 125 µm³; A/V = 1.2 µm⁻¹. With side 10 µm, A/V = 6/10 = 0.6 µm⁻¹. Exchange area per volume halves, potentially reducing exchange capacity relative to metabolic demand if all else is equal.

questions.prompt: Describe one structural adaptation and its physiological benefit for each type I and type II pneumocyte in human alveoli. Predict what happens to surface tension when type II surfactant secretion falls.
questions.answer: Type I cells are extremely thin, reducing gas diffusion distance; type II cells contain lamellar-body secretory vesicles and release surfactant into the alveolar lumen. Lower surfactant secretion raises surface tension and predisposes alveoli to collapse.

Relate thinness to reduced diffusion distance.

Predict reduced surfactant leads to greater surface tension/collapse tendency.
